governanceNotes: D1 batch 56 (2026-09-25): two bounded association edges authored - loss-of-testicle to hypogonadism (rank 1) and to depressive-disorder (rank 2) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true. The hypogonadism proposition rests on the torsion cohort documenting higher LH and FSH with lower testosterone after orchiectomy versus orchiopexy (PMID 42676052) and the systematic review and meta-analysis documenting significantly increased FSH and LH and reduced sperm concentration with testosterone preserved by hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal compensation (PMID 42546903). The depressive-disorder proposition rests on the mental-health systematic review quantifying psychological impacts and management strategies (PMID 41050387) and the 240-versus-240 comparative study documenting poorer genital self-image and greater dissatisfaction (PMID 41212238).

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-25: (i) the meta-analysis found testosterone levels comparable between orchiectomy and orchiopexy through compensatory mechanisms, so the endocrine signal is gonadotropin elevation and impaired spermatogenesis in mostly unilateral loss rather than universal overt testosterone deficiency; (ii) the torsion cohort found erectile function did not differ between orchiectomy and orchiopexy despite hormonal differences, dissociating the erectile limb from the androgen limb; (iii) the psychological literature mixes malignancy and non-malignancy indications with the cancer diagnosis itself as a depressogenic exposure; (iv) testosterone replacement and antihormonal therapy alter both limbs.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Orchiectomy documents disruption of gonadal endocrine function: the testicular-torsion cohort found that patients who underwent orchiectomy had significantly higher luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormone levels and lower testosterone than patients who underwent orchiopexy (PMID 42676052), and the systematic review and meta-analysis of 538 torsion patients found orchiectomy associated with significantly increased FSH and LH and reduced sperm concentration versus testis-sparing surgery (PMID 42546903); the co-occurrence is documented at cohort and systematic-review class, so the edge records endocrine-risk only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the located material documents gonadotropin elevation and testosterone change after orchiectomy, but unilateral versus bilateral loss, contralateral testicular function, replacement therapy, timing, and pituitary status all require individual review before any causal statement.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Removal of testicular tissue eliminates part of the androgen-producing gonadal mass, raising pituitary gonadotropins and lowering testosterone reserve toward compensated or overt hypogonadism, the endocrine shift documented after orchiectomy, but whether any individual hypogonadism arose from a given orchiectomy remains hypothesized until serial hormone records and replacement-therapy history are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at cohort and systematic-review class: the meta-analysis found testosterone levels comparable between orchiectomy and orchiopexy due to hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal compensation in mostly unilateral loss, so the documented signal is gonadotropin elevation and reduced sperm concentration rather than universal overt testosterone deficiency, and bilateral loss is differently represented.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The meta-analysis found testosterone comparable between orchiectomy and orchiopexy through hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal compensation in mostly unilateral loss; bilateral loss is differently represented and replacement therapy alters every measure.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: primary hypogonadism from other testicular disease
obesity and metabolic suppression of testosterone

evidenceGaps: The meta-analysis found testosterone comparable between orchiectomy and orchiopexy through hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal compensation in mostly unilateral loss; bilateral loss is differently represented and replacement therapy alters every measure.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the endocrine-consequence precedent: the testicular-torsion surgical cohort found that orchiectomy patients had higher luteinizing hormone (P < 0.001) and follicle-stimulating hormone (P = 0.009) with lower testosterone (P = 0.008) than orchiopexy patients (PMID 42676052), and the systematic review and meta-analysis of eleven studies with 538 participants found orchiectomy associated with significantly increased FSH (SMD 1.63) and LH (SMD 1.31) and reduced sperm concentration versus orchiopexy, while testosterone and inhibin-B remained comparable through compensatory hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal mechanisms (PMID 42546903); because the evidence is mostly unilateral-loss class where compensation preserves circulating testosterone, the documented signal is gonadotropin elevation and impaired spermatogenesis rather than universal overt deficiency, and replacement therapy alters every measure, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through dated serial hormone panels with unilateral-versus-bilateral documentation and competing-cause exclusion.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Orchiectomy documents psychological impact independent of the endocrine limb: the systematic review of mental health after orchiectomy synthesizes the literature quantifying psychological impacts and stratifying cultural and demographic influences, with testosterone replacement and cognitive behavioural therapy both appearing as management strategies (PMID 41050387), and the 240-versus-240 matched comparative study documents significantly poorer genital self-image and greater sexual dissatisfaction in orchiectomized men with self-image correlating to mood-relevant psychosocial domains (PMID 41212238); the co-occurrence is documented at systematic-review and comparative-cohort class, so the edge records psychological-impact risk only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the located material documents psychological burden after orchiectomy, but the malignancy indication, fertility grief, body-image distress, hormonal contribution, cultural context, and pre-existing psychiatric history all require individual review before any causal statement.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Loss of a sexual gland drives body-image distress, fertility grief, and altered masculine self-perception that elevate depressive-symptom burden alongside the parallel androgen-deficiency pathway, the psychological impact quantified in post-orchiectomy mental-health synthesis, but whether any individual depressive disorder arose from a given orchiectomy remains hypothesized until psychiatric, hormonal, and psychosocial records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at systematic-review and comparative-cohort class: the reviewed literature mixes cancer and non-cancer indications with the malignancy diagnosis itself as a major depressogenic exposure, most cohorts lack pre-operative psychiatric baselines, and part of the mood signal runs through androgen deficiency which is separately windowed.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Most reviewed cohorts lack pre-operative psychiatric baselines and mix malignancy with non-malignancy indications; part of the mood signal runs through androgen deficiency, which is separately windowed.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: depressive disorder from the malignancy indication itself

evidenceGaps: Most reviewed cohorts lack pre-operative psychiatric baselines and mix malignancy with non-malignancy indications; part of the mood signal runs through androgen deficiency, which is separately windowed.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the disfigurement-and-loss psychosocial precedent, scoped to the psychological-impact limb with an explicit pathway distinction from the androgen limb: the systematic review of mental health after orchiectomy synthesizes the available literature to quantify psychological impacts, explore cultural and demographic influences, and present management strategies including testosterone replacement, cognitive behavioural therapy, and social support (PMID 41050387), and the comparative study of 240 orchiectomized men versus 240 age-matched controls found significantly lower genital self-image, sexual-satisfaction, and ejaculatory-control scores with elevated dissatisfaction in the orchiectomy group (PMID 41212238); because the reviewed literature mixes malignancy and non-malignancy indications with the cancer diagnosis itself as a depressogenic exposure, most cohorts lack pre-operative psychiatric baselines, and the androgen-deficiency limb is separately windowed on the hypogonadism edge, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through dated psychiatric documentation with indication, hormonal status, and pre-morbid history recorded and competing-cause exclusion.
